meta.title: Who really said "Do not wait to strike till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not W. B. Yeats. The exact line first appears unsigned in an 1853 American quotation book. The earliest known form is Benjamin Franklin's, 1782.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do not wait to strike till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking'?
meta.ogDescription: Yeats got the credit in 1997, on Usenet. The wording is an unsigned entry in an 1853 quotation book; the earliest known form is Franklin's, 1782.

answer.label: Not William Butler Yeats — an unsigned 1853 maxim
answer.sourceLine: No Yeats poem, play, essay or letter contains this sentence, and it appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Yeats page ↗, which records no disputed or misattributed quotations for him at all. The exact wording first turns up in 1853, on page 227 of an American anthology called The World’s Laconics, filed under the heading ‘Promptness and energy’ and — unlike the signed entry above it — carrying no author’s name at all. That is twelve years before Yeats was born. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the extended metaphor further back still, to a letter Benjamin Franklin wrote in 1782, and finds the Yeats credit appearing for the first time in 1997, in a quote-of-the-day post on Usenet.

source.excerpt:
Promises.—We promise according to our hopes, but perform according to our fears.—Rochefoucauld.

Promptness and energy.—Do not wait to strike, till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking.

Promptness and energy.—“How,” said one to Sir W. Raleigh, of whom it was said he “could toil terribly,”—“how do you accomplish so much, and in so short a time?” “When I have anything to do, I go and do it,” was the reply.
trail: The proverb it extends is ancient; Chaucer already has men smiting while the iron is hot. The extension — heat the iron yourself — has an earliest known instance that is unexpectedly precise: a letter from Benjamin Franklin to the Reverend Richard Price, dated Passy, 13 June 1782, printed at page 96 of William Morgan’s Memoirs of the Life of The Rev. Richard Price (1815). Franklin is writing about the power of the press, and closes the thought: ‘it is not only right to strike while the iron is hot, but that it may be very practicable to heat it by continually striking’ the 1815 volume ↗.

Cromwell enters by accident. In Lacon (1821) the English cleric Charles Caleb Colton wrote that a policy which can strike only while the iron is hot ‘will be overcome by that perseverance, which, like Cromwell’s, can make the iron hot by striking’ — naming Cromwell as an example of persistence, not as the author of a phrase. Later compilers dropped the distinction and printed the words as Cromwell’s outright. The sentence can be read at page 47 of an early American edition Lacon, New York 1824, from the eighth London edition ↗.

The wording everyone now quotes is set in 1853, in The World’s Laconics: Or, The Best Thoughts of the Best Authors, compiled by Tryon Edwards under the pen name Everard Berkeley, with an introduction by the Presbyterian minister William B. Sprague. On page 227, under ‘Promptness and energy’, it stands alone with no credit at all the scanned volume ↗. Sprague’s name is on the title page as the writer of the introduction — and Sprague is who later gets the credit.

Yeats arrives late and from nowhere. The first attribution to him that Quote Investigator can locate is a Usenet message of 7 June 1997 in alt.quotations, headed ‘Creative Quotations for Jun 13 from William Butler Yeats’. The subject line is a date-of-the-day format, and Yeats was born on 13 June. A newspaper columnist in Appleton, Wisconsin repeated the credit in February 2000, and it circulates under his name on quote sites today the full investigation ↗.
source.excerptNote: Page 227 of The World’s Laconics, as printed. The entry above it carries an author’s name — Rochefoucauld, Goldsmith, Sir W. Temple, Tillotson, Washington all appear on the surrounding pages — and this one carries none, in a book whose own subtitle is The Best Thoughts of the Best Authors. Note also the comma the compiler set after ‘strike’, which the modern circulating version drops.

source.rightsNote: Both sources that matter here are long out of copyright in the United States. The earliest known printing of this exact wording is an American book of 1853, where it stands unsigned; the earliest known form of the metaphor is a Franklin letter of 1782, published in 1815. Anything first published before 1931 is in the US public domain, so the sentence is free to reproduce, and no author or estate has ever been in a position to claim it. The only real constraint is factual rather than legal: do not print it over the name of W. B. Yeats — or of Cromwell, either Sprague, Lamb or Hemingway. This is not legal advice.

author.name: W. B. Yeats
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Yeats
author.metaLine: 1865–1939 · Irish poet, dramatist and Nobel laureate (1923)
author.bio: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was an Irish poet and dramatist, a leading figure of the Irish Literary Revival, a co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, and the winner of the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature. He is also a standing magnet for unsourced wisdom: brisk, encouraging one-liners with no owner drift onto his name because he is famous, quotable, Irish and long dead. The tell here is register. Yeats wrote about gyres and swans and Byzantium; a blacksmith’s maxim about seizing the initiative sounds nothing like him, and no edition of his work contains it. The line reached his name in 1997, fifty-eight years after he died, by way of a Usenet quote-of-the-day post.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with no owner, and it shows. Since the 1850s it has been handed to at least six different people, not one of whom has ever been shown to have written it. Quote Investigator lays out the whole procession, decade by decade.

items.why: No poem, play, essay, letter or manuscript has ever been produced, and the line is absent from Wikiquote’s Yeats page ↗, which records no disputed or misattributed quotations for him at all. The wording was already in print in 1853, twelve years before Yeats was born, and the first credit to him is a Usenet quote-of-the-day post from 1997.

items.who: Named as an example, not as the author
items.why: Charles Caleb Colton’s Lacon (1821) invokes ‘that perseverance, which, like Cromwell’s, can make the iron hot by striking’ — Cromwell is the model of persistence in Colton’s sentence, not its speaker. By 1878 The Bee-Keeper’s Magazine was printing the words as something Cromwell said outright Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

items.who: Wrote the introduction, not the line
items.why: Sprague’s name is printed on the 1853 title page as the author of the book’s introduction; the saying itself sits unsigned on page 227 the scanned volume ↗. By 1989, William Safire and Leonard Safir’s Words of Wisdom: More Good Advice was printing the line over Sprague’s name.

items.scope: Peleg Sprague, Charles Lamb, Ernest Hemingway
items.why: An 1850 filler item in the Fayetteville Observer gave a version to Peleg Sprague — a different Sprague entirely; an 1895 dental trade journal handed it to Charles Lamb; and in January 1964 Playboy ran ‘It is good policy to strike while the iron is hot. It is better still to make the iron hot by striking’ in a set of aphorisms bylined Ernest Hemingway. None of the three carries a source the full chronology ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it. The oldest printing of this exact sentence is an unsigned entry on page 227 of an 1853 American quotation book; the oldest known form of the thought is Franklin’s, in a letter of 13 June 1782. As Quote Investigator concludes, many names have been attached over the years, but the supporting evidence has been ‘scanty’ read the investigation ↗.

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: The sentence is built to be repeated. It takes a proverb everyone already knows — strike while the iron is hot — and turns it inside out with a semicolon. You do not wait for the moment; you manufacture it. That structure is why it has survived 170 years of being handed from name to name: it is memorable enough to carry itself, and short enough that nobody feels the need to check where it came from.

It is also, quietly, the perfect shape for an orphan. A saying that arrives in print already unsigned has no defender and no estate, so every generation is free to give it to whoever seems most likely. In the nineteenth century that meant a soldier famous for relentlessness, then an essayist; in the twentieth, a novelist, and finally a poet. Yeats got it last, in 1997, from a birthday-keyed quotation feed — and, because the internet copies rather than checks, that is where it has stayed.
context.detailsSummary: What Franklin was actually talking about
detailsBody: Franklin’s 1782 version is not a self-help line at all. Writing to the Reverend Richard Price from Passy, just after the fall of Lord North’s ministry, he is making an argument about the printing press as an instrument of politics: the Greek and Roman orators ‘could only speak to the number of citizens capable of being assembled within the reach of their voice’, whereas ‘now by the press we can speak to nations’.

The iron follows directly from that. Repeating the same truths daily, in different lights, in newspapers that are everywhere read, is what makes it ‘very practicable to heat it by continually striking’. In its original setting the metaphor is about propaganda and public opinion, not personal initiative — the motivational reading is what the next two centuries did to it.
context.pull: A maxim about seizing the initiative, printed in 1853 with nobody’s name on it — in a book subtitled The Best Thoughts of the Best Authors.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's chronology: the exact wording 'Do not wait to strike, till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking' first appears without attribution in Tryon Edwards's 1853 The World's Laconics (p. 227); the earliest full match for the extended metaphor is Franklin's 1782 letter to Richard Price; Colton's 1821 Lacon names Cromwell as an example, not the author; the first credit to William Butler Yeats is a 7 June 1997 Usenet post in alt.quotations headed 'Creative Quotations for Jun 13 from William Butler Yeats', repeated by a Post-Crescent columnist on 28 February 2000; QI concludes many names have been linked but 'the supporting evidence has been scanty'. Also documents credits to Peleg Sprague (1850 Fayetteville Observer), Charles Lamb (1895 Items of Interest), William B. Sprague (Safire, Words of Wisdom, 1989) and Ernest Hemingway (Playboy, January 1964).

The scanned 1853 first edition (M. W. Dodd, New York; title page reads 'BY EVERARD BERKELEY ... WITH AN INTRODUCTION BY WILLIAM B. SPRAGUE, D.D.') prints on page 227, under the heading 'Promptness and energy', the entry 'Do not wait to strike, till the iron is hot ; but make it hot by striking.' with no author credited — while the entry immediately above it is credited to Rochefoucauld, and Goldsmith, Sir W. Temple and other names are credited on the surrounding pages. (Not every neighbouring entry is signed: the second 'Promptness and energy' item directly below, the Sir W. Raleigh anecdote, is itself unsigned.)

William Morgan's Memoirs of the Life of The Rev. Richard Price (1815) prints, at pages 95–96, a letter headed 'Passy, June 13, 1782' from Dr. Franklin containing: 'And we now find that it is not only right to strike while the iron is hot, but that it may be very practicable to heat it by continually striking', in a passage about newspapers and the power of the press ('Now by the press we can speak to nations').

Colton's Lacon (this copy: New-York, printed by E. Marks, 1824, 'from the eighth London edition') prints at page 47, in section LXVIII: 'That policy that can strike only while the iron is hot, will be overcome by that perseverance, which, like Cromwell's, can make the iron hot by striking; and he that can only rule the storm, must yield to him who can both raise and rule it.'

Wikiquote's W. B. Yeats page does NOT contain 'Do not wait to strike till the iron is hot; but make it hot by striking' in any section. The page's only top-level sections are 'Quotes', 'Quotes about Yeats' and 'External links' — it has no 'Disputed' or 'Misattributed' section at all.
William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet, dramatist, writer and literary critic, born 13 June 1865 and died 28 January 1939; he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923.

Tryon Edwards (7 August 1809 – 4 January 1894) was an American theologian and minister best known for his collection of quotations, A Dictionary of Thoughts. NOTE: this Wikipedia article does NOT mention The World's Laconics or the 'Everard Berkeley' pseudonym — those come from Quote Investigator and from the 1853 title page itself, and no claim about them is attached to this link.
